steps.title: Requirements
steps.goal: Agree on what to build and what 'good' means before drawing anything.
checklist: List 3-5 core functional requirements; park the rest out loud
Ask about scale: DAU, read/write ratio, data size, regions
Pin the non-functionals: latency target, availability, consistency, durability
Write assumptions down where the interviewer can see them

steps.title: Back-of-the-envelope
steps.goal: Turn scale into QPS, storage and bandwidth so the design has numbers to defend.
checklist: QPS = daily requests / 86,400 (≈ 10^5 s); peak ≈ 2-3× average
Storage = items/day × size × retention × replication factor
Bandwidth = QPS × payload size
Say which number drives the design (e.g. reads ≫ writes → cache)

steps.title: API
steps.goal: Define the contract the clients use; it fixes the scope of the rest.
checklist: 3-6 endpoints or RPCs with inputs and outputs
Pagination (cursor), idempotency keys on writes, auth
Sync vs async: which calls return 202 and finish later

steps.title: Data model
steps.goal: Choose entities, keys and the store that fits the access pattern.
checklist: Entities and their primary/partition keys
Access patterns first, then SQL vs NoSQL vs blob vs search
Indexes, and how the largest table is partitioned

steps.title: High-level design
steps.goal: Draw the boxes that satisfy every functional requirement end to end.
checklist: Client → edge (DNS/CDN/LB) → stateless services → data stores
Walk one write path and one read path through the diagram
Add queues where work can be async; caches where reads dominate

steps.title: Deep dives & trade-offs
steps.goal: Go deep on the 2-3 hardest parts and name what you'd trade.
checklist: Bottlenecks and hot spots: hot keys, celebrity users, fan-out
Failure modes: what happens when each box dies; retries, idempotency
Consistency choices and why; what you'd monitor (SLOs, alerts)

latency.label: Round trip in the same data centre

rubric.label: Clarified requirements and wrote down what's out of scope
Estimated QPS, storage and bandwidth, and used them in a decision
Defined a clear API including pagination and idempotency
Picked stores from access patterns and explained partition keys
High-level diagram covers every functional requirement end to end
Found the real bottleneck (hot key, fan-out, write amplification…) and fixed it
Covered failure modes: retries, timeouts, replicas, degraded mode
Named trade-offs explicitly (consistency vs latency, cost vs freshness…)
Mentioned observability: metrics, SLOs, alerts, dashboards
Finished inside 45 minutes with time for deep dives

blocks.name: Load balancer
blocks.summary: Spreads requests across stateless servers and removes unhealthy ones.
tradeoffs: L4 is fast and protocol-agnostic; L7 can route by path/header and retry, but costs more CPU
Sticky sessions simplify state but unbalance load and break on failover
blocks.pitfall: Forgetting the LB itself needs redundancy (active-passive pair or managed LB) and health checks that test real dependencies, not just a 200 from /.

blocks.name: Cache (Redis / Memcached)
blocks.summary: Keeps hot data in memory to cut read latency and database load.
tradeoffs: Cache-aside is simple but serves stale data until TTL or invalidation
Write-through keeps the cache fresh at the cost of write latency
More memory vs lower hit rate
blocks.pitfall: Cache stampede when a hot key expires: use request coalescing, jittered TTLs or early refresh. And never cache private data in a shared layer.

blocks.name: CDN
blocks.summary: Serves static and cacheable content from edge locations near users.
tradeoffs: Pull CDNs are easy but the first request misses; push gives control but you manage uploads
Long TTLs are cheap but invalidation is slow
blocks.pitfall: Bad cache keys: including cookies or random query params destroys the hit rate. Version asset URLs instead of purging.

blocks.name: Message queue / log (Kafka, SQS)
blocks.summary: Decouples producers from consumers so slow or failing work doesn't block requests.
tradeoffs: Kafka keeps an ordered, replayable log per partition; SQS-style queues are simpler but don't replay
At-least-once delivery means consumers must be idempotent
blocks.pitfall: Ordering only holds within a partition: choose the partition key (user id, order id) so related events stay together.

blocks.name: Sharding (partitioning)
blocks.summary: Splits a dataset across nodes by a key so storage and writes scale horizontally.
useWhen: One node can't hold the data or the write rate
tradeoffs: Range partitioning supports scans but creates hot ranges; hash partitioning spreads load but loses range queries
Cross-shard joins and transactions get expensive
blocks.pitfall: A low-cardinality or skewed key (country, celebrity user) makes one shard hot. Plan resharding before you need it.

blocks.name: Replication
blocks.summary: Copies data to multiple nodes for availability, durability and read scaling.
useWhen: You can't lose data when a node dies
tradeoffs: Leader-follower is simple; async replicas can serve stale reads
Multi-leader and leaderless (quorum) raise availability but need conflict resolution
blocks.pitfall: Read-your-writes: a user writes to the leader and reads a lagging replica. Route their reads to the leader for a short window.

blocks.name: Consistent hashing
blocks.summary: Maps keys to nodes on a ring so adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys.
tradeoffs: Virtual nodes smooth the distribution but add metadata
Rendezvous hashing is simpler for small clusters
blocks.pitfall: Without virtual nodes a few physical nodes own huge arcs of the ring and become hot.

blocks.name: Rate limiting
blocks.summary: Caps requests per client per window to protect services and share capacity fairly.
tradeoffs: Token bucket allows bursts; sliding-window log is exact but memory-heavy; fixed windows are cheap but spiky at edges
Central counters (Redis) are accurate but add a hop; local limits are fast but approximate
blocks.pitfall: Non-atomic read-then-write counters race under load. Use INCR with expiry or a Lua script.

blocks.name: Search index (Elasticsearch / OpenSearch)
blocks.summary: Inverted index for full-text search, filtering and relevance ranking.
tradeoffs: Near-real-time, not transactional: index asynchronously from the source of truth
Great reads, costly writes and reindexing
blocks.pitfall: Using the search index as the primary database. Keep the DB as truth and rebuild the index from it (CDC).

blocks.name: Blob / object store (S3)
blocks.summary: Cheap, durable storage for large immutable objects like images, video and backups.
useWhen: Files larger than a few hundred KB
tradeoffs: Very durable and cheap, but higher latency than block storage
Strong read-after-write now, but no partial in-place updates
blocks.pitfall: Proxying uploads through your app servers. Hand clients pre-signed URLs and upload directly.

blocks.name: Observability
blocks.summary: Metrics, logs and traces that tell you whether the system meets its SLOs and why not.
useWhen: Always; mention it in every design
tradeoffs: High-cardinality metrics and full tracing are powerful but expensive; sample
Push vs pull metrics collection
blocks.pitfall: Alerting on causes (CPU 80%) instead of symptoms users feel (error rate, p99 latency against the SLO).

blocks.name: Unique ID generation
blocks.summary: Creates globally unique, ideally time-sortable IDs without a central bottleneck.
tradeoffs: Snowflake (time + machine + sequence) sorts by time but needs worker-id assignment and clock care
UUIDv4 is coordination-free but random (bad index locality); UUIDv7/ULID are time-ordered
blocks.pitfall: Clock skew or NTP jumps backwards can duplicate Snowflake IDs; refuse to issue IDs until the clock catches up.

cases.title: URL shortener (bit.ly)
cases.summary: Turn long URLs into short codes and redirect billions of clicks with low latency.
functional: Create a short URL for a long URL (optional custom alias and expiry)
Redirect a short URL to the original
Basic click analytics per link
nonFunctional: Redirect p99 < 50 ms
99.99% available for redirects
Codes must not collide; not easily guessable
Read-heavy: ~100:1 reads to writes
estimates: 100M new URLs/month ≈ 40 writes/s; 100:1 reads ≈ 4k redirects/s, peak ~10k
5 years × 1.2B/yr = 6B URLs × 500 B ≈ 3 TB
7 Base62 chars = 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes, plenty
api: POST /v1/urls {longUrl, alias?, expiresAt?} → 201 {code, shortUrl}
GET /{code} → 302 Location: longUrl (or 404/410)
GET /v1/urls/{code}/stats → {clicks, byDay[]}
dataModel: urls(code PK, long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at) in a KV/wide-column store partitioned by code
clicks events → Kafka → aggregated counts per code per day
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U["Client"] --> LB["Load balancer"]
  LB --> API["Shortener API"]
  API --> KGS["Key generator"]
  API --> DB[("URL store")]
  LB --> R["Redirect service"]
  R --> C[("Redis cache")]
  C -. miss .-> DB
  R --> K["Kafka: clicks"]
  K --> AGG["Stream aggregator"]
  AGG --> ST[("Stats store")]

deepDives.title: Generating codes
deepDives.body: Hashing the URL (MD5 → first 7 Base62 chars) needs collision checks. A global counter encoded in Base62 is collision-free but predictable and a single point of failure. A key-generation service that pre-allocates ranges of IDs to each API node (or Snowflake IDs → Base62) gives uniqueness without a hot counter.

deepDives.title: 301 vs 302
deepDives.body: 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect, cutting load but hiding repeat clicks from analytics. 302 keeps every click visible. Most shorteners use 302 when analytics matter.

deepDives.title: Read path
deepDives.body: Redirects dominate, so put a cache (Redis or CDN edge) in front of the store with a long TTL. The mapping is immutable, so invalidation only happens on delete/expiry.

deepDives.title: Analytics without slowing redirects
deepDives.body: Emit a click event asynchronously to Kafka and return the redirect immediately; aggregate per minute/day in a stream job.

tradeoffs: Counter vs hash vs KGS for codes
302 + analytics vs 301 + lower load
Strong uniqueness on create vs eventual consistency for stats
probes: How do you avoid two nodes issuing the same code?
What happens when a hot link goes viral?
How do you stop people enumerating codes?
How would you support custom aliases safely?

cases.title: Distributed key-value store (Dynamo)
cases.summary: A highly available, partitioned KV store with tunable consistency.
functional: put(key, value) and get(key)
Values up to ~1 MB
Configurable replication factor
nonFunctional: Always writable (AP) with tunable consistency
Scale horizontally to hundreds of nodes
p99 < 10 ms in-region
Survive node and rack failures
estimates: 10 TB data, RF=3 → 30 TB raw; ~100 nodes at 300 GB each
100k ops/s → ~1k ops/s per node
api: PUT /kv/{key} body=value, header consistency=ONE|QUORUM|ALL
GET /kv/{key} → value + version (vector clock)
dataModel: Each node: LSM tree (memtable + SSTables + commit log)
Ring metadata: token → node, shared by gossip
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C["Client"] --> CO["Coordinator node"]
  CO --> N1["Replica A"]
  CO --> N2["Replica B"]
  CO --> N3["Replica C"]
  N1 <-. gossip .-> N2
  N2 <-. gossip .-> N3
  N1 --> L1[("LSM storage")]
  N2 --> L2[("LSM storage")]
  N3 --> L3[("LSM storage")]

deepDives.title: Partitioning
deepDives.body: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes places each key on the ring; the next N distinct nodes clockwise hold replicas. Adding a node moves only its share of keys.

deepDives.title: Quorums
deepDives.body: With N replicas, writes wait for W acks and reads for R. R + W > N gives overlapping sets, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write. N=3, W=2, R=2 is the common balance.

deepDives.title: Failures
deepDives.body: Gossip spreads membership and suspicion. Sloppy quorum plus hinted handoff keeps writes flowing when a replica is down; read repair and Merkle-tree anti-entropy fix divergence later.

deepDives.title: Conflicts
deepDives.body: Concurrent writes produce siblings. Vector clocks detect them; resolve with last-write-wins (simple, loses data) or app-level merge (shopping cart union).

tradeoffs: Consistency vs availability per request (R/W)
LWW simplicity vs merge correctness
LSM write speed vs read/compaction cost
probes: What does R + W > N guarantee, exactly?
How does a node learn another is dead?
What is hinted handoff and when does it fail?
How do you rebalance when adding nodes?

cases.title: Distributed rate limiter
cases.summary: Limit requests per user/IP/API key across a fleet of gateways.
functional: Rules like 100 req/min per API key, 5 logins/min per IP
Return 429 with Retry-After and remaining-quota headers
Rules change without deploys
nonFunctional: Adds < 2 ms to each request
Accurate within a few percent under concurrency
Fail open if the limiter store is down (configurable)
estimates: 1M active keys × ~100 B state ≈ 100 MB in Redis
50k req/s → 50k Redis ops/s: one shard, or a few for headroom
api: Middleware: allow(key, rule) → {allowed, remaining, resetAt}
Admin: PUT /rules/{id} {match, limit, window}
dataModel: Redis key per (rule, client): token count + last refill time, with TTL
Rules in a config store cached in each gateway
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C["Client"] --> GW["API gateway + limiter"]
  GW -- "Lua: take token" --> R[("Redis cluster")]
  GW -- allowed --> S["Backend services"]
  GW -- "429 + Retry-After" --> C
  CFG[("Rules config")] -. cached .-> GW

deepDives.title: Algorithms
deepDives.body: Token bucket (refill rate r, capacity b) allows bursts up to b; leaky bucket smooths output; fixed window is cheap but allows 2× at window edges; sliding-window log is exact but stores every timestamp; sliding-window counter approximates it with two buckets.

deepDives.title: Atomicity
deepDives.body: Read-modify-write from many gateways races. A Redis Lua script (or INCR + EXPIRE) makes take-a-token atomic in one round trip.

deepDives.title: Scale and latency
deepDives.body: Shard Redis by key. For very hot paths, keep a local token bucket per gateway that syncs with Redis periodically: approximate, but no network hop.

deepDives.title: Failure policy
deepDives.body: If Redis is unreachable, fail open for most APIs (availability) but fail closed for login/OTP endpoints (security).

tradeoffs: Exactness vs memory (log vs counters)
Central accuracy vs local speed
Fail open vs fail closed
probes: How do you keep two gateways from both granting the last token?
Where does the limiter live: client, gateway, service?
How would you limit by multiple dimensions at once?
What headers do you return?

cases.title: Unique ID generator (Snowflake)
cases.summary: Generate unique, roughly time-ordered 64-bit IDs at high rate without coordination.
functional: Return a unique 64-bit ID per call
IDs sort roughly by creation time
nonFunctional: 10k+ IDs/s per node, < 1 ms
No single point of failure
Unique across data centres
estimates: 41 bits of ms timestamp ≈ 69 years
10 bits machine id = 1,024 workers; 12 bits sequence = 4,096 IDs/ms per worker
api: nextId() → int64 (in-process library or tiny service)
dataModel: Layout: 1 sign | 41 timestamp ms since custom epoch | 5 DC | 5 worker | 12 sequence
Worker ids leased from ZooKeeper/etcd or config
cases.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S1["Service A"] --> G1["ID worker 1"]
  S2["Service B"] --> G2["ID worker 2"]
  G1 -. "lease worker id" .-> Z[("etcd / ZooKeeper")]
  G2 -. "lease worker id" .-> Z
  G1 --> T["timestamp | dc | worker | seq"]

deepDives.title: Options
deepDives.body: DB auto-increment is simple but a bottleneck and leaks volume. Ticket servers (Flickr) use two DBs with odd/even IDs. UUIDv4 needs no coordination but is 128-bit and random, hurting B-tree locality. UUIDv7/ULID add a time prefix. Snowflake fits 64 bits and sorts by time.

deepDives.title: Clock problems
deepDives.body: If NTP moves the clock backwards, a worker could reissue IDs. Detect it and wait (or refuse) until time passes the last issued timestamp.

deepDives.title: Sequence overflow
deepDives.body: More than 4,096 IDs in one millisecond: spin until the next millisecond.

tradeoffs: 64-bit compactness vs coordination for worker ids
Time-ordering vs leaking creation time and volume
Random UUIDs vs index locality
probes: Why not just use UUIDv4?
What happens if the clock goes backwards?
How are worker ids assigned and reclaimed?

cases.title: Notification system
cases.summary: Send push, SMS and email reliably at scale while respecting user preferences.
functional: Services send notifications to users over push, SMS and email
Users choose channels and quiet hours
Templates with localisation
Scheduled and bulk campaigns
nonFunctional: Soft real-time: < 5 s for transactional messages
At-least-once delivery, no visible duplicates
Survive provider outages (APNs/FCM/Twilio/SES)
estimates: 10M push + 1M SMS + 5M email per day ≈ 200 msgs/s average, bursts of 50k/s for campaigns
api: POST /v1/notifications {userIds|segment, template, data, channels?, idempotencyKey}
PUT /v1/users/{id}/preferences
dataModel: preferences(user_id, channel, enabled, quiet_hours)
devices(user_id, token, platform)
notification_log(id, user_id, channel, status, attempts) for dedup and audit

deepDives.title: Decoupling by channel
deepDives.body: One queue per channel isolates failures: an SMS provider outage doesn't stall push. Workers scale independently.

deepDives.title: Retries and dedup
deepDives.body: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter; after N attempts park the message in a DLQ. An idempotency key + delivery log stops duplicates when a worker crashes after sending.

deepDives.title: Preferences and rate limits
deepDives.body: Check opt-outs and quiet hours before enqueueing; cap per-user frequency so a bug can't spam people.

tradeoffs: At-least-once + dedup vs exactly-once (not really achievable end to end)
Fan-out at send time vs per-segment batch jobs
Single vs multiple providers per channel
probes: How do you avoid sending the same push twice?
What happens when APNs is down for an hour?
How do you send to 50M users in a campaign?

cases.title: News feed (Twitter / Instagram)
cases.summary: Build each user's home timeline from the people they follow, fast.
functional: Post (text/media)
Follow users
Home timeline of followed users' posts, newest or ranked
nonFunctional: Timeline load p99 < 200 ms
New posts visible to followers within ~5 s
Read-heavy (≈ 100:1)
estimates: 300M DAU × 5 timeline loads = 1.5B reads/day ≈ 17k/s, peak 50k/s
50M posts/day ≈ 600 writes/s; average 200 followers → 120k timeline inserts/s with fan-out on write
api: POST /v1/posts {text, mediaIds}
GET /v1/timeline?cursor=…&limit=20
POST /v1/users/{id}/follow
dataModel: posts(post_id snowflake, author_id, text, media, created_at) sharded by author
follows(follower_id, followee_id) both directions
timeline cache: Redis list of post ids per user (last ~800)

deepDives.title: Fan-out on write vs read
deepDives.body: Push: on post, insert the id into every follower's cached timeline; reads are O(1) but writes explode for celebrities. Pull: build the timeline at read time by merging followees' recent posts; cheap writes, slow reads. Hybrid: push for normal users, pull celebrities' posts at read time and merge.

deepDives.title: Timeline cache
deepDives.body: Store only post ids in Redis lists, capped in length; hydrate post bodies from a post cache. Inactive users' timelines can be rebuilt on demand.

deepDives.title: Ranking
deepDives.body: Fetch a candidate set (a few hundred ids), score with a model (recency, affinity, engagement), and return the top N with a cursor.

tradeoffs: Write amplification vs read latency
Freshness vs cost for inactive users
Chronological simplicity vs ranked engagement
probes: What happens when someone with 100M followers posts?
How do you paginate a ranked feed without duplicates?
How do deletes propagate?

cases.title: Chat (WhatsApp / Slack)
cases.summary: 1:1 and group messaging with delivery receipts, offline sync and presence.
functional: 1:1 and group chats (≤ 500 members)
Sent / delivered / read receipts
Offline delivery and multi-device sync
Online presence
nonFunctional: Message delivery p99 < 500 ms when online
No message loss; per-chat ordering
Hundreds of millions of concurrent connections
estimates: 100M DAU × 40 messages = 4B/day ≈ 46k msgs/s
100 B per message → 400 GB/day; years of history → PB scale
Each gateway holds ~500k WebSocket connections → ~200 gateways
api: WebSocket: send {chatId, clientMsgId, body} → ack {msgId, seq}
WebSocket push: message, receipt, presence events
GET /v1/chats/{id}/messages?before=seq
dataModel: messages(chat_id partition, seq clustering, sender, body, ts) in Cassandra/ScyllaDB
connection registry: user_id → gateway id (Redis)
per-device last-read seq

flowchart LR
  A["Sender"] <--> GW1["WS gateway 1"]
  B["Recipient"] <--> GW2["WS gateway 2"]
  GW1 --> CS["Chat service"]
  CS --> DB[("Messages store")]
  CS --> REG[("Connection registry")]
  CS --> GW2
  CS -. offline .-> PN["Push notifications"]
  GW1 --> PR["Presence service"]

deepDives.title: Routing messages
deepDives.body: Gateways keep long-lived WebSockets. The chat service persists the message, assigns a per-chat sequence number, then looks up the recipient's gateway in the registry and forwards. If offline, send a push and let the client sync on reconnect.

deepDives.title: Ordering and dedup
deepDives.body: Clients send a clientMsgId; the server dedups retries and assigns a monotonic per-chat seq. Clients render by seq and fetch gaps.

deepDives.title: Storage
deepDives.body: Partition by chat id with seq as clustering key so a chat's history is one sequential read. Discord moved from Cassandra to ScyllaDB for this access pattern.

deepDives.title: Presence
deepDives.body: Heartbeats every ~30 s update a TTL key; fan presence out only to contacts currently online, and batch it for large groups.

tradeoffs: WebSockets vs long-polling
Per-chat ordering vs global ordering
Storing on server vs end-to-end encryption limits
probes: How does a message find the right gateway?
How do you guarantee no loss if a gateway crashes?
How does a phone that was offline for a week catch up?

cases.summary: Upload, transcode and stream video worldwide with adaptive bitrate.
functional: Upload videos
Transcode to multiple resolutions/codecs
Stream with adaptive bitrate
View counts
nonFunctional: Playback start < 2 s; minimal rebuffering
Uploads durable; processing within minutes
Egress cost dominates: maximise CDN offload

1B views/day; egress handled almost entirely by CDN

GET /v1/videos/{id}/manifest.m3u8
POST /v1/videos/{id}/views (batched)

deepDives.title: Transcoding pipeline
deepDives.body: Split the upload into chunks, transcode chunks in parallel into a bitrate ladder (240p…4K, H.264/VP9/AV1), package into HLS/DASH segments of 2-6 s, then publish the manifest.

deepDives.title: Adaptive bitrate
deepDives.body: The player measures throughput and buffer and switches renditions segment by segment. Short segments adapt faster; long segments compress better.

deepDives.title: CDN strategy
deepDives.body: Popular titles are pre-positioned in ISP-embedded caches (Netflix Open Connect); the long tail is pulled on demand. View counts are batched client-side and aggregated asynchronously.

tradeoffs: More renditions vs storage/compute cost
Segment length: adaptivity vs efficiency
Pre-positioning vs pull-through caching
probes: Why chunk the transcode?
How does the player pick a bitrate?
How do you count views without hammering a DB?

cases.summary: Match riders with nearby drivers in real time and track the trip.
functional: Drivers stream location every few seconds
Riders request a ride and get matched to a nearby driver
Trip lifecycle and live tracking
Fare estimate and surge
nonFunctional: Match in < 5 s
Location ingest of millions of updates/s
Trip state must never be lost or double-assigned
estimates: 5M active drivers × 1 update/4 s ≈ 1.25M writes/s (in-memory only)
~100k ride requests/min at peak

POST /v1/rides {pickup, dropoff} → rideId
GET /v1/rides/{id} (or WS updates)

trips(id, rider, driver, state, timestamps) in a strongly consistent DB

deepDives.title: Geo indexing
deepDives.body: Geohash prefixes, quadtrees or Uber's hexagonal H3 cells map a point to a cell; search the rider's cell plus neighbours (k-ring) for available drivers, then rank by ETA, not straight-line distance.

deepDives.title: Location ingest
deepDives.body: Updates are ephemeral: keep the latest position per driver in memory (sharded by city/cell), and stream to Kafka for analytics. Don't write every ping to a database.

deepDives.title: Matching without double-booking
deepDives.body: Offer to one driver at a time with a short timeout; claim the driver with a conditional update (driver.state = available → reserved) so two riders can't get the same driver.

tradeoffs: Hexagons (uniform neighbours) vs geohash (simple prefixes)
Greedy nearest match vs batch-optimised matching
In-memory speed vs durability for locations
probes: How do you find drivers within 2 km quickly?
How do you stop two riders getting one driver?
What's the trip state machine?

cases.title: Payment system
cases.summary: Accept payments exactly once, keep a correct ledger and reconcile with providers.

deepDives.title: Per-user pub/sub channels and fan-out
deepDives.body: Every user owns a Redis pub/sub channel. When user A connects, her WebSocket server subscribes to the channel of each of her online, opted-in friends. When A publishes a location, the location service writes it to her own channel once and Redis delivers it to every subscribed gateway, which pushes to the friends' sockets. Fan-out is therefore done by subscription, not by the application looping over friends. Redis pub/sub is at-most-once and keeps no history, which is exactly right here because the next update arrives in 30 s anyway. Shard channels across a Redis cluster by user id with consistent hashing, and manage membership changes (friend comes online, goes offline, opts out) by subscribe/unsubscribe calls.

deepDives.title: Distance filter and cache with TTL
deepDives.body: A publish carries the sender's position but the radius check is done by the receiving side: the gateway computes the distance between the new point and the subscriber's last cached location and only pushes if it is within the radius. The location cache (loc:{userId}) is overwritten on each ping and has a TTL slightly above two update intervals, so inactive users expire without a cleanup job. On connect, the client's init handler reads the cache for all friends in a pipelined batch to render the first screen. Distance uses the haversine formula, which is cheap enough to run per delivery.

deepDives.title: WebSocket gateway and connection management
deepDives.body: Stateful gateways hold the sockets; a load balancer with sticky routing during the upgrade assigns the connection and each gateway handles perhaps 50k-100k idle sockets. Heartbeats detect dead mobile connections, and on reconnect the client sends its last known timestamp so out-of-order or duplicate updates are discarded by ts. Deploys drain gateways gradually to avoid a reconnect storm, with jittered backoff on the client. Keeping the location service stateless behind the gateway means we scale it by adding pods.

deepDives.title: Geohash vs quadtree for the nearby places sibling problem
deepDives.body: A related question is 'find places or users near a point' without a friend graph. A geohash encodes lat/lng into a base32 string where shared prefixes mean nearby cells, so it indexes cleanly in any ordered or key-value store, and a radius query scans the point's cell plus its 8 neighbours. Its weakness is edge cases at cell boundaries and uneven density. A quadtree adaptively splits a cell into four when it holds too many points, so dense downtown areas get small cells and rural ones stay large, but it is an in-memory tree that must be rebuilt or kept in sync. Systems like S2 and H3 improve cell uniformity. Friends lookup does not need either because the friend list bounds the candidate set.

deepDives.title: Map tiles: raster vs vector and the tile pyramid
deepDives.body: The world is cut into a pyramid: zoom level z has 2^z × 2^z tiles, each addressed by z/x/y. Raster tiles are pre-rendered images, simple to serve but heavy and fixed in style. Vector tiles ship geometry and attributes (protobuf) and the client renders them, which gives smaller payloads, smooth zoom, rotation, restyling and dark mode. Low zooms are pre-generated and pushed to a CDN with long cache lifetimes; very high zooms are rendered lazily on first request and cached. Tiles are immutable per map version, so cache invalidation is by versioned URLs.

deepDives.title: Routing on the road graph and why hierarchies
deepDives.body: Roads are a weighted directed graph: intersections are nodes, segments are edges with travel-time cost. Dijkstra is correct but explores a huge region for long trips; A* with a geographic heuristic (straight-line time at max speed) prunes the search, and bidirectional search helps more. At global scale even that is too slow, so production systems preprocess the graph: contraction hierarchies add shortcut edges that skip unimportant nodes, so a query climbs up to highway-like nodes and down again, touching a few thousand nodes in milliseconds. A related approach is hierarchical routing by road class (local roads near the endpoints, highways in the middle). The cost is preprocessing time and memory, and live traffic weights complicate precomputed shortcuts, so customisable variants re-weight shortcuts quickly.

deepDives.title: Graph partitioning into regions
deepDives.body: The graph is split into geographic regions or cells (for example with balanced min-cut partitioning), each small enough to hold in memory on one routing node. Within a region, routing is exact; across regions the router uses precomputed boundary nodes and shortcut distances between them, then stitches the segments. Hot regions get more replicas. Updating the map (new road, closed bridge) only rebuilds the affected partition and its boundary shortcuts, and routing nodes swap in the new version atomically.

deepDives.title: ETA, live traffic and rerouting
deepDives.body: Navigation clients stream location and speed to an ingestion service, which snaps points to road edges (map matching) and writes to Kafka. A stream job aggregates average speed per edge per few-minute window into the live traffic store. The ETA service sums edge times using live speeds for the near future and historical speeds by time-of-day and weekday for edges further along the route, because traffic will have changed by the time you get there. Active sessions are tracked per affected edges, so when a significant slowdown appears on a route the rerouting service recomputes and pushes a new route over the WebSocket if it saves enough time to justify distracting the driver.

tradeoffs: Vector tiles (small, flexible, client does work) vs raster tiles (simple, heavy)
Exact shortest path (Dijkstra) vs fast heuristic or preprocessed routing (A*, contraction hierarchies) with a rebuild cost
Precomputing shortcuts (fast queries) vs real-time traffic weights that invalidate them
Reroute eagerly (better ETA) vs rarely (less flip-flopping and server load)
Pre-render all tiles (storage cost) vs render on demand (cold-start latency)

deepDives.title: Why an append-only log is fast
deepDives.body: Messages are appended to the end of a segment file, so the broker does purely sequential writes, which disks and SSDs handle at near hardware speed. The OS page cache buffers recent writes and serves reads of recent data from memory, so brokers lean on the kernel instead of maintaining their own cache. Consumers reading the tail mostly hit the page cache, and sending to the network uses zero-copy (sendfile) to move bytes from the page cache straight to the socket without copying through user space. Batching and compression amortise per-message overhead, which is the main throughput lever.

deepDives.title: Replication, ISR and producer acks
deepDives.body: Each partition has a leader and followers; followers fetch from the leader like consumers. The in-sync replica set (ISR) is the leader plus followers that are caught up within a lag threshold. With acks=0 the producer does not wait, acks=1 waits for the leader only (a leader crash can lose acked data), and acks=all waits for every ISR member. Combining acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 and replication factor 3 tolerates one broker failure without data loss, and refuses writes rather than risk loss if the ISR shrinks too far. The controller elects a new leader from the ISR on failure, so no acknowledged message is lost.

deepDives.title: Consumer groups, offsets and rebalancing
deepDives.body: Within a group each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so parallelism is capped by the partition count. A group coordinator tracks members through heartbeats; when a member joins, leaves or times out, a rebalance reassigns partitions, and during the classic protocol consumers pause. Incremental cooperative rebalancing and static membership reduce the disruption. Consumers commit the offset of the next message to read to the internal offsets topic; committing before processing yields at-most-once, after processing yields at-least-once with possible duplicates.

deepDives.title: Delivery semantics and what exactly-once really means
deepDives.body: At-most-once means possible loss, at-least-once means possible duplicates, and the network cannot give true exactly-once delivery between independent systems. What is offered is effectively-once processing: idempotent producers (producer id plus sequence number per partition) deduplicate retried batches at the broker, and transactions let a consumer-process-produce loop atomically write output records and commit its input offsets, so read-process-write within the log is exactly-once. Anything that touches an outside system (a database, an email) still needs idempotent consumer logic or a transactional outbox. Ordering is only guaranteed within a partition, so records that must stay ordered share a key.

tradeoffs: Throughput and batching vs per-message latency (linger and batch size settings)
acks=all durability vs write latency and availability when the ISR shrinks
More partitions (more parallelism) vs more open files, longer leader elections and rebalancing cost
Delete retention (bounded storage) vs log compaction (latest value per key, state rebuild)
Pull-based consumers (backpressure, replay) vs push-based brokers (lower latency, flow control complexity)

deepDives.title: Push vs pull collection
deepDives.body: In pull mode (Prometheus style) a collector scrapes each target's /metrics endpoint on a schedule using service discovery. It makes health obvious (a failed scrape means the target is down), is easy to debug with a browser, and keeps targets simple, but it needs network reachability and struggles with short-lived jobs, which use a push gateway. In push mode agents or SDKs send batches to a collector, which works across NAT and firewalls and for batch jobs, but needs backpressure and rate limits so a misbehaving client cannot flood the system. Large systems often combine them: local agents scrape or receive on the host, then push batched data into Kafka, which decouples collectors from storage and absorbs spikes.

deepDives.title: Time-series storage and compression
deepDives.body: General databases are poor at this write pattern, so a purpose-built TSDB keeps recent samples in memory (with a WAL for crash recovery) and periodically writes immutable compressed blocks. Timestamps arrive at nearly regular intervals, so storing the delta of deltas turns most into a single zero bit; floating-point values are XOR-ed with the previous one so unchanged or similar values compress to a few bits, as described in Facebook's Gorilla paper. An inverted index maps label pairs to series ids, so a query like service=api AND status=500 intersects postings lists. Blocks are time-partitioned, which makes retention a cheap file delete and lets queries skip irrelevant blocks.

deepDives.title: High cardinality pitfalls
deepDives.body: Every unique label combination creates a new series, so a label such as user_id, request_id or a full URL path multiplies series count and memory (each active series costs index and head-block memory), slowing ingestion and queries, and can take the system down. Mitigations are labels limited to bounded sets, per-tenant series quotas, dropping or aggregating offending labels at the collector, and putting per-request detail into logs or traces instead of metrics. Churn (series that appear and vanish, such as per-pod labels on frequently redeployed containers) is a second form of the same problem.

deepDives.title: Query layer, downsampling and alerting
deepDives.body: A query service fans a query out to the relevant shards and time blocks, merges the results, and caches common dashboard queries by time-aligned step. Old data is rolled up asynchronously to coarser resolutions keeping min, max, sum and count, and the query layer picks the resolution that fits the requested step. The alert evaluator runs rules on a schedule against recent data; a rule must be true for a 'for' duration before firing, which suppresses blips. The alert manager then deduplicates identical alerts from replicated evaluators, groups related ones into one notification, applies silences and inhibition (do not page for pods when the node is down), routes by labels to the right on-call channel and rate-limits repeats to avoid flapping spam.

tradeoffs: Pull (central control, simple targets) vs push (works for short-lived jobs and across firewalls)
Kafka buffer (resilient to spikes, adds latency and cost) vs writing directly to the TSDB
Raw retention (full fidelity, expensive) vs downsampled rollups (cheap, lose spikes and exact percentiles)
Rich labels (flexible queries) vs cardinality cost: enforce quotas and review new labels
Short alert 'for' windows (fast detection) vs flapping and false pages

How do you avoid paging 50 times when one database dies?
How would you make the TSDB multi-tenant and horizontally scalable?

deepDives.title: Inbound pipeline
deepDives.body: Remote servers find us through the recipient domain's MX records and connect to a stateless fleet of SMTP edge servers behind a load balancer. The edge applies cheap checks first: connection rate limits, IP blocklists, reverse DNS, recipient exists. Then it runs SPF (is this IP allowed to send for the MAIL FROM domain), DKIM (verify the signature over the headers and body against the key in DNS) and DMARC (does the From domain align with an SPF or DKIM pass, and what policy does the domain request). Content filters (virus scan, ML spam score) are heavier and run asynchronously from a queue. The key rule is to reply 250 only after the raw message is written durably to a queue or the blob store, so a crash after the reply cannot lose it; a temporary failure should return 4xx so the sender retries.

deepDives.title: Outbound queue, retries and bounces
deepDives.body: Submission servers authenticate the user, sign the message with DKIM, and write one queue row per recipient domain so a slow domain does not block others. Sender workers look up the domain's MX records, pick a warmed IP from a pool, and speak SMTP with TLS. A 4xx reply or a timeout reschedules the row with exponential backoff (for example 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, up to 3 to 5 days); a 5xx is a hard bounce that stops retrying and generates a DSN (non-delivery report) into the sender's mailbox. Per-domain concurrency caps and rate limits protect us from being throttled by Gmail-sized receivers. Bounce and spam-complaint feedback loops update a suppression list so we stop mailing addresses that keep failing, which protects IP reputation.

deepDives.title: Mailbox storage and partitioning
deepDives.body: All the access patterns are per user (list a folder, fetch by UID, set flags), so partition the metadata by user_id and never need cross-user transactions. A wide-column store (Cassandra or Bigtable style) with the clustering key (folder, received_at DESC) gives cheap newest-first pagination; sharded MySQL works too if you want transactions for flag and move operations. Large bodies and attachments are immutable, so they live in the blob store keyed by content hash, which also allows deduplication of the same attachment sent to many recipients. A heavy user is one big partition, so cap partition size by bucketing on (user_id, month) for very large mailboxes. IMAP UIDs need a per-folder monotonic counter, which is a good reason to keep a folder's writes on one partition owner.

deepDives.title: Search and threading
deepDives.body: Each delivered message emits an event that an indexer consumes to update a per-user inverted index (shards co-located by user so a query touches one shard, not a scatter-gather). Index only text fields and keep the original body in the blob store; rebuild the index from the event log or the stored messages if a shard is lost. Threading is done at delivery time: if In-Reply-To or References matches a Message-ID we already stored for the user, reuse that thread_id; otherwise fall back to a normalised subject match within a time window, and otherwise start a new thread. Eventual consistency is acceptable here, as search can lag delivery by seconds.

tradeoffs: Accept then filter asynchronously (higher throughput, risk of backscatter bounces) vs filter fully before the 250 reply (slower SMTP dialogue, simpler semantics)
Wide-column store (easy horizontal scale, weak multi-row transactions) vs sharded SQL (transactions for moves and flags, harder resharding)
Inline small bodies in the metadata row (faster open) vs always use blob pointers (smaller hot set, extra hop)
Per-user search shards (cheap queries, uneven shard sizes) vs global index (simple, expensive scatter-gather)
Aggressive spam filtering (cleaner inboxes) vs false positives that lose legitimate mail

deepDives.title: Data store and metadata store are separate systems
deepDives.body: Splitting them lets each scale on its own axis: metadata is small, hot and needs ordered range scans and strong consistency; data is huge, cold and needs sequential bandwidth. A PUT streams the bytes to the data plane first, which returns an object_id and checksum; only after the bytes are durable does the metadata service commit the (bucket, key, version) row pointing at it. That ordering means a crash leaves an orphan blob (cleaned by GC) but never a metadata row pointing at nothing. Data nodes pack many small objects into large append-only files with an in-memory index, because one file per object would exhaust inodes and cause random IO. Metadata strong read-after-write is reached with consensus replication inside each metadata shard, so a list after a PUT sees the new key.

deepDives.title: Replication vs erasure coding and the durability math
deepDives.body: 3x replication stores three full copies: 200% overhead, simple reads from any copy, cheap repair (copy one replica). Erasure coding 8+4 splits an object into 8 data and 4 parity fragments on 12 different failure domains (disks, racks, zones); any 8 of 12 reconstruct the object, so it survives 4 simultaneous losses at only 50% overhead. The costs are CPU for encode and decode, higher read latency when a data fragment is missing (degraded reads), and repair that reads 8 fragments to rebuild 1. Durability comes from the independent-failure assumption plus repair speed: durability is about how fast you restore redundancy before further failures stack up, so spread fragments across racks and zones and prioritise repair of the most-degraded stripes. Common practice is replication or small-object packing for hot, small data and erasure coding for large, cold data.

deepDives.title: Placement, rebalancing, checksums and repair
deepDives.body: A placement manager (or consistent hashing over placement groups) maps each object to a group of nodes, tracking node health through heartbeats. When disks are added or fail, only the affected placement groups move, throttled so rebalancing does not starve foreground traffic. Every object and fragment carries a checksum verified on write, on read and by a background scrubber that walks all disks slowly, catching silent bit rot before multiple fragments are bad. A corrupt or missing fragment is rebuilt from the surviving ones onto a healthy node and the placement map is updated. End-to-end checksums supplied by the client (Content-MD5 or SHA-256) catch corruption in the network path too.

deepDives.title: Multipart upload, versioning, listing and garbage collection
deepDives.body: Multipart upload lets clients upload parts in parallel and retry only failed parts. Each part is stored as its own data object; Complete atomically writes a single metadata row whose data pointer is the ordered part list, so no data is copied. Abandoned uploads are expired by a lifecycle rule. With versioning on, a DELETE just inserts a delete marker row; real bytes are removed only when a specific version is deleted or a lifecycle rule expires it. Because deleted, overwritten and aborted objects leave orphaned data, a garbage collector compares the metadata store with the data nodes (or consumes a delete queue), waits a safety delay, then compacts the append-only files to reclaim space. Listing at scale relies on key-ordered range partitions: a prefix plus delimiter query becomes a range scan that skips whole common-prefix ranges, and continuation tokens encode the last key returned.

tradeoffs: Replication (fast, simple repair, 3x cost) vs erasure coding (about 1.5x cost, CPU and repair amplification)
Range partitioning by key (ordered listing, hot-prefix risk) vs hash partitioning (even load, expensive listing)
Packing small objects into big files (efficient, needs compaction and an index) vs one file per object (simple, wasteful)
Strong consistency for metadata (consensus latency on every write) vs eventual consistency (faster, surprising clients)
Aggressive GC (reclaims space sooner) vs safety delay (protects against bugs and races at the cost of storage)
probes: What happens if the data write succeeds and the metadata commit fails, or the reverse?
A whole rack goes down. How do you keep serving reads and how do you repair?

cases.title: Digital wallet / ledger
cases.summary: Move money between wallets at high throughput with exactly-once effect, an auditable double-entry ledger and a balance that never goes negative.
functional: Transfer money from one wallet to another
Read a wallet's current balance
List a wallet's transaction history with pagination
Top up from and withdraw to an external payment provider
Full audit trail and the ability to reconstruct any balance at any point in time
nonFunctional: Exactly-once effect: a retried or duplicated request moves money once
Strong consistency and a hard invariant: balance never below zero, total money conserved
Reliable under crashes, retries and partial failure, with no lost or invented money
Auditable and reproducible: every balance can be explained from immutable records
High throughput with p99 transfer latency under a few hundred ms
estimates: Assume 100M wallets and 1B transfers/day ≈ 12k/s average; design for ~100k/s peak (about 8x, Black Friday style)
Assume one tuned relational primary sustains about 1k to 2k transfer transactions/s (two row updates plus ledger inserts plus fsync); 100k/s then needs about 50 to 100 shards, each with replicas
Per transfer: 1 transfer row + 2 ledger entries + 1 idempotency row ≈ 0.7 KB, so 1B/day ≈ 700 GB/day ≈ 250 TB/year before replication and indexes
Balance reads are typically 5 to 10x writes: serve from the wallet row (or a read replica or cache for non-critical views), never by summing history
Hot wallets (a large merchant, 1% of traffic = 1k/s on one row) exceed single-row update capacity of roughly 1k/s, so they need special handling
api: POST /v1/transfers {fromWalletId, toWalletId, amount: 2500, currency: "USD"} with Idempotency-Key header returns 201 {transferId, status} (amount in minor units, integer)
GET /v1/transfers/{transferId} returns {status: pending|completed|failed, ...} so clients can resolve an unknown outcome
GET /v1/wallets/{walletId}/balance returns {available, pending, asOfSeq}
GET /v1/wallets/{walletId}/entries?cursor=...&limit=50 returns ledger entries newest first
POST /v1/wallets/{walletId}/topups {amount, source} with Idempotency-Key and POST /v1/wallets/{walletId}/withdrawals {amount, destination}
POST /webhooks/provider (signed) for external settlement events
dataModel: wallets(wallet_id PK, owner_id, currency, balance BIGINT CHECK (balance >= 0), version, updated_at) sharded by hash of wallet_id
transfers(transfer_id PK, idempotency_key UNIQUE, request_hash, from_wallet, to_wallet, amount, status, created_at) co-located with the source wallet shard
ledger_entries(entry_id, transfer_id, wallet_id, direction DEBIT or CREDIT, amount, balance_after, created_at) append-only, two entries per transfer that sum to zero
event log: events(wallet_id, seq, type, payload, created_at) with UNIQUE (wallet_id, seq) giving optimistic concurrency; the source of truth in an event-sourced variant
outbox(event_id, payload, published_at) written in the same DB transaction, relayed to Kafka for read models and notifications
reconciliation_runs(run_id, shard, checked_through_seq, mismatches) recording the periodic audit

deepDives.title: Exactly-once effect with idempotency keys
deepDives.body: Networks give at-least-once delivery, so exactly-once must be built from at-least-once plus idempotency. The client generates a unique Idempotency-Key per logical transfer and reuses it on every retry. The server inserts the key with a hash of the request in the same DB transaction that applies the money movement, guarded by a UNIQUE constraint; a duplicate key either returns the stored result or, if the request hash differs, a 422. Because the dedup row and the balance change commit atomically, a crash cannot leave one without the other. The transfer status endpoint lets a client that timed out discover whether the transfer happened instead of blindly retrying with a new key.

deepDives.title: Same-shard vs cross-shard transfers: 2PC, TCC and Saga
deepDives.body: If both wallets live on one shard, a single local ACID transaction does the debit, credit, two ledger entries and idempotency row, and `UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - :amt WHERE id = :from AND balance >= :amt` enforces never-negative without a read-modify-write race. Across shards, 2PC gives atomicity but holds locks across a coordinator round trip and blocks if the coordinator dies, so it hurts throughput and availability. TCC reserves first (Try: move the amount into a hold on the source), then Confirm or Cancel, so no long locks and each step is idempotent. A Saga runs local transactions (debit source, then credit destination) with compensations (refund the source if the credit fails), persisting saga state so a recovery worker can resume or compensate after a crash. Money systems usually prefer TCC or a Saga with an explicit pending state so an observer never sees money vanish, and each step must be idempotent and retried until it succeeds.

deepDives.title: Event sourcing, CQRS and replay
deepDives.body: In the event-sourced variant the append-only event log (TransferInitiated, Debited, Credited) is the source of truth and balances are folded from it. Commands are validated against the current state, then append events with an expected sequence number, which gives optimistic concurrency per wallet. A deterministic state machine means anyone replaying the log from the beginning (or from a snapshot) reaches the same balances, which makes audits, debugging and rebuilding corrupted views straightforward. CQRS separates the write path (commands appended to the log) from read models (balance, history, search) built asynchronously from the event stream, so reads scale independently but may lag slightly; the balance used for the never-negative check must come from the write side. Raft or a consensus-replicated log makes the event store durable and strongly ordered for each partition.

deepDives.title: Hot wallets and reconciliation
deepDives.body: A single row can only absorb about one transaction's worth of lock time at once, so a merchant wallet receiving thousands of credits per second becomes a bottleneck. Credits are commutative, so split such a wallet into N sub-balance rows (a sharded counter), crediting a random sub-row and debiting by drawing from sub-rows, with the logical balance being their sum; or batch credits into a single aggregated update every few milliseconds. Whatever the design, run reconciliation continuously: assert that every transfer's entries sum to zero, that each wallet's balance equals the sum of its entries, and that totals match the external provider's settlement files. Discrepancies raise alerts and are fixed with compensating entries, never by editing history.

tradeoffs: Single-shard transactions (simple, fast) vs spreading wallets for scale (cross-shard transfers need Saga or TCC)
2PC (strong atomicity, locks and blocking coordinator) vs Saga or TCC (non-blocking, intermediate states and compensation logic)
Balance column plus ledger (fast reads, two things to keep consistent) vs balance only derived from events (single truth, slower reads unless projected)
Event sourcing (perfect audit and replay, operational complexity, schema evolution) vs a mutable-row design with an append-only ledger table
Sharded sub-balances for hot wallets (throughput) vs a simple single row (exact and simple but a hard ceiling)
probes: The debit succeeded and the service crashed before the credit. What does the user see and how does recovery work?
How do you guarantee two concurrent transfers cannot overdraw one wallet?
How would you find and fix a 1 cent discrepancy between your ledger and the bank?
How do you reshard wallets from 50 to 100 shards while transfers are running?
How do you handle transfers across currencies or to a wallet owned by another region?

cases.title: Stock exchange matching engine
cases.summary: Match buy and sell orders fairly and deterministically in microseconds, publish market data and survive failures without losing or reordering a single order.
functional: Place limit and market orders (buy or sell) for a listed symbol
Cancel an open order
Match orders by price-time priority and report fills (executions) to both sides
Publish real-time market data: order book depth, last trade, best bid and offer
Pre-trade risk checks: funds or position limits, price bands, order size
nonFunctional: Very low latency: order-to-acknowledgement in tens of microseconds, with a tight, predictable p99
Deterministic and fair: the same input sequence always produces the same output
Highly available with fast failover and no lost accepted orders
Complete audit trail: every event is stored and replayable for regulators
Throughput of tens to hundreds of thousands of orders per second, scaling by symbol
estimates: Assume 100 symbols and 1B orders/day over a 6.5 hour session (23,400 s): ≈ 43k orders/s average, ~200k/s at the open or on news (assumption of roughly 5x)
Assume 100 B per order event: 1B x 100 B ≈ 100 GB/day for the sequenced event log, tiny compared to the budget of the matching hardware

The LMAX architecture article reports about 6 million orders/s on one business-logic thread, so one thread per symbol group easily covers the load; the hard part is latency and determinism, not raw throughput

Latency budget (assumption): gateway decode and risk about 5 to 10 us, sequencer about 1 to 3 us, matching about 1 to 5 us, publishing to the outbound path a few us, so wire-to-wire of well under 100 us

Market data fan-out: each book update is sent to every subscriber; with 1,000 subscribers and 100k updates/s that is 100M messages/s, so use multicast or per-feed fan-out servers rather than the engine itself
api: FIX NewOrderSingle (or a binary protocol such as OUCH/SBE): {clOrdId, symbol, side: BUY|SELL, ordType: LIMIT|MARKET, price (integer ticks), qty, timeInForce: DAY|IOC|FOK}
FIX OrderCancelRequest {origClOrdId, symbol, side} and OrderCancelReplace for amend (amend that increases size loses time priority)
ExecutionReport (server to client): {orderId, execType: NEW|TRADE|CANCELED|REJECTED, lastQty, lastPx, leavesQty, cumQty}
REST for broker and retail front ends: POST /v1/orders {symbol, side, type, price, qty} with Idempotency-Key; DELETE /v1/orders/{orderId}; GET /v1/orders?status=open
Market data stream: subscribe {symbols[], depth: L1|L2} delivering incremental updates {seq, symbol, side, price, qty} plus periodic snapshots to recover from gaps
GET /v1/marketdata/{symbol}/candles?interval=1m&from=...&to=... served from a separate analytics store
dataModel: In-memory order book per symbol: bids and asks as price-sorted structures (sorted tree or an array indexed by price tick) where each price level holds a doubly linked FIFO list of orders
orderIndex: hash map orderId -> pointer to the node in its price level, giving O(1) cancel; best bid and best ask pointers are cached so a match is O(1) at the top of the book
Order: {orderId, symbol, side, price in integer ticks, qty, leavesQty, accountId, enteredSeq}; use integers for prices and quantities, never floating point
Sequenced event log (append-only, memory-mapped file or journal): {seq, timestamp, eventType, orderId, symbol, payload}; the source of truth that the book can be rebuilt from, plus periodic snapshots
Downstream stores: orders, executions and positions in a relational database for clearing and reporting; candles and history in a time-series store

deepDives.title: Order book and price-time priority matching
deepDives.body: Each symbol has a buy side (bids, best = highest price) and a sell side (asks, best = lowest price); an order matches the opposite side while prices cross. Priority is price first, then arrival time: orders at one price level wait in a FIFO list, and the earliest gets filled first. A new limit order walks the opposite side's best levels, producing trades at the resting order's price, and any unfilled remainder rests in the book; a market order takes whatever liquidity is available until filled (or rejected if none); IOC cancels the unfilled part and FOK fills entirely or not at all. Use a sorted map or a tick-indexed array for price levels, a linked list per level for O(1) append and removal, and an orderId hash map so a cancel is O(1) rather than a book scan.

deepDives.title: Sequencer, event sourcing and determinism
deepDives.body: A single sequencer stamps every inbound event (new order, cancel) with a monotonically increasing sequence number and writes it to the journal before the engine processes it. The matching engine is a deterministic state machine: it uses only the sequenced events (no wall-clock reads, random numbers or thread races) so replaying the same log from the same snapshot reproduces identical trades. That gives fairness (one global order), auditability, easy testing and crash recovery by replay. Keeping the matching logic single-threaded avoids locks entirely; concurrency lives around it in the gateway, risk and network IO.

deepDives.title: LMAX Disruptor style pipeline and hot standby
deepDives.body: Inside the engine, stages (receive and unmarshal, journal, replicate, match, publish) are connected by a pre-allocated ring buffer with sequence-number coordination instead of locked queues, avoiding allocation, garbage collection pauses and cache-line contention; threads are pinned to cores and the hot path touches only data in CPU cache. Journaling and replication run in parallel with the business logic stage so durability does not add serial latency. For availability, a hot standby consumes the same sequenced stream and maintains an identical book; if the primary's heartbeat stops, a leader election (Raft or an external arbiter) promotes the standby, which has no state to load. Fencing is critical so a paused or partitioned primary cannot keep emitting trades.

deepDives.title: Market data, risk checks and scaling by symbol
deepDives.body: Risk checks sit before the sequencer and must be cheap and in-memory: validate account state, buying power or position limits, price collars against the last trade, fat-finger size limits and a kill switch. The engine emits an outbound stream of events that a market data publisher converts into incremental L2 updates and trade prints with their own sequence numbers; clients detect gaps and request a snapshot. Distribution uses UDP multicast inside the exchange or per-feed fan-out servers so the engine never talks to individual subscribers. Because one symbol's orders never interact with another's, scale horizontally by assigning symbol groups to separate sequencer and engine pairs; hot symbols get their own engine, and cross-symbol products (spreads, baskets) need extra coordination.

tradeoffs: Single-threaded matching (deterministic, no locks, one core's throughput) vs multi-threaded matching (harder, nondeterministic ordering)
Synchronous replication to standby before acknowledging (no lost orders, added microseconds) vs asynchronous (faster, risk of losing the last events on failover)
Sorted tree for price levels (flexible, O(log n)) vs tick-indexed array (O(1) but needs bounded price ranges)
Heap and garbage-collected language convenience vs pre-allocated memory and off-heap structures for stable tail latency
Multicast market data (cheap, unreliable, needs gap recovery) vs TCP fan-out (reliable, higher latency and cost per subscriber)
probes: How do you guarantee that two orders arriving at the same microsecond are processed in the same order after a restart?
The primary matching engine crashes mid-batch. What does the standby do and what happens to in-flight orders?
How would you handle an order cancel racing with a fill for the same order?
How do you shard when one symbol alone exceeds one engine's capacity?
How would you support market-wide halts, opening and closing auctions or circuit breakers?
